Our central finding is a statistically significant crossover interaction between normalization type and gradient flow ($p{<}0.05$): BatchNorm with gradient flow is the only configuration that maintains or improves collision avoidance, while removing gradient flow causes catastrophic representational drift. Surprisingly, LayerNorm with gradient flow consistently \emph{degrades} safety below the no-auxiliary-head baseline, making it the worst configuration tested. Gradient flow benefits are thus BatchNorm-mediated, not an intrinsic property of auxiliary gradients.
Same-seed gradient analysis reveals the mechanism: LayerNorm redistributes gradient magnitude across vision backbones, suppressing spatial encoder gradients while amplifying semantic encoder gradients. This cross-backbone gradient redistribution, not representation corruption, explains the safety degradation and constitutes a representation-behavior dissociation where representational fidelity does not predict safety. Label content (structured, random, depth) does not affect outcomes when gradient flow is maintained.
Practical guidelines: maintain BatchNorm with gradient flow; if gradient flow is unavailable, substitute LayerNorm to prevent drift; never combine LayerNorm with gradient flow. The auxiliary head is discarded after training at zero inference cost.

Gradient norms, CKA, and behavioral metrics converge on a crossover interaction account: BN and gradient flow interact (7.3\,pp, Table~\ref{tab:factorial}) rather than compose additively. When gradient flow calibrates BN running statistics, coupling is beneficial (Full OCC); without calibration, BN statistics drift, causing catastrophic representational corruption (Detach OCC CKA $\downarrow$0.31--0.54). This manifests the known BN sensitivity to distribution shift~\cite{ioffe2015batchnorm, li2017adabn, schneider2020bn} as a training-time phenomenon.

The crossover is most striking in Full OCC+LN (Table~\ref{tab:factorial}): gradient flow with LayerNorm produces the \emph{worst} safety behavior despite preserving pretrained representations (CKA $\geq$0.95), a representation-behavior dissociation. Same-seed gradient analysis (Section~\ref{sec:gradient_dynamics}) identifies the mechanism as cross-backbone gradient redistribution rather than representation corruption, ruling out intrinsic behavioral regularization~\cite{lee2015deeply, pezeshki2021gradient}. Gradient flow benefits are predominantly BN-mediated: BN maintains balanced gradient allocation that LN disrupts.

\textbf{Practical guideline.} Maintain BatchNorm with gradient flow; if gradient flow is unavailable, substitute LayerNorm; never combine LayerNorm with gradient flow. No ground-truth labels needed; the head is discarded at zero inference cost, complementing runtime safety methods~\cite{hu2025vlsa, raja2024ogmcbf}. Limitations are discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:limitations}.
tool_args.new_string:
The ordinal interaction pattern---gradient flow is detrimental and BatchNorm amplifies the damage---has two notable properties. First, the damage is independent of spatial content: Full OCC, Random OCC, and Depth all achieve comparable CAR, indicating that the gradient pathway, not the spatial information, determines safety outcomes. Second, the Cell~1 instability ($\sigma{=}0.064$, $3{\times}$ other cells) suggests that BN + gradient flow creates a volatile optimization landscape where seed-dependent outcomes range from near-Vanilla to catastrophic ($\Delta{=}-11.4$\,pp for the worst seed).

Gradient analysis confirms orthogonality between action and auxiliary gradients (cosine $\approx$ 0, conflict rate $\approx$ 50\%), ruling out direct gradient conflict as the mechanism~\cite{yu2020pcgrad, liu2021cagrad}. The detrimental effect of gradient flow operates through indirect channels---likely reshaping the LoRA optimization trajectory under a dual-objective loss landscape~\cite{lippl2024implicit, jiang2023forkmerge}---rather than through gradient interference.

\textbf{Practical guideline.} Do not add auxiliary spatial heads for the purpose of improving collision avoidance; all tested configurations perform at or below the Vanilla baseline. If an auxiliary head is required by other objectives, use detached gradients with LayerNorm (Detach+LN), and never combine BatchNorm with gradient flow. No ground-truth spatial labels are needed; the head is discarded at zero inference cost, complementing runtime safety methods~\cite{hu2025vlsa, raja2024ogmcbf}. Figure~\ref{fig:gradient_analysis} reveals a gradient collapse mechanism underlying the Detach degradation. All gradient norms are computed with respect to the L1 action loss (action tokens only), not the full language modeling objective. Action loss gradient norms are comparable across Vanilla and gradient-flow conditions (0.87--1.14$\times$ Vanilla norms), which rules out gradient amplification. Detach OCC, however, exhibits catastrophic collapse: encoder gradient norms fall to 1--13\% of Vanilla across all layers (action gradient norm 0.005 vs.\ Vanilla 0.126, a 25$\times$ reduction). Per-layer analysis (Figure~\ref{fig:per_layer_combined}, Appendix) decomposes auxiliary gradient flow into amplitude and direction: Detach collapses uniformly while gradient-flow conditions maintain Vanilla-comparable norms; DINOv2 layers show $\sim$50\% conflict rate while SigLIP late layers (blocks 21--24) drop to 19--25\%, which indicates cooperative alignment. Both patterns are identical for structured and random labels. The crossover interaction (Section~\ref{sec:mechanism}) reveals that gradient flow's collapse-prevention effect is BN-mediated: under LN, gradient flow degrades rather than improves CAR.

\textbf{LN induces cross-backbone gradient redistribution.} Same-seed analysis (seed 42, four conditions, 200 batches at 50K checkpoint) reveals why LayerNorm with gradient flow degrades CAR. Under Full OCC+LN, action loss gradients in DINOv2 are suppressed 3.5$\times$ relative to BN (mean norm 0.048 vs.\ 0.168), while SigLIP action gradients are amplified 2.5$\times$ (0.206 vs.\ 0.081). Conflict rates remain ${\sim}$50\% in both conditions, which rules out directional conflict as the cause. The mechanism is cross-backbone amplitude redistribution: LN normalization redistributes gradient magnitude from DINOv2 to SigLIP, disrupting the balanced allocation that BN maintains (DINOv2: 0.8$\times$ Vanilla, SigLIP: 1.0$\times$ Vanilla). This explains why Full OCC+LN degrades CAR despite preserving pretrained representations: the problem is not \emph{what} the encoders represent, but \emph{how} gradient flow allocates learning signal across them.
